```{r setup, include=FALSE}
library(tidyverse)

knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  message = FALSE,
  fig.width = 7,
  fig.asp = 0.65,
  out.width = "100%"
)

theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 12) + theme(legend.position = "bottom"))
```

## Problem 1: Shared birthdays

I assume 365 equally likely birthdays and independent birthdays across
people. The function below samples birthdays with replacement and returns
whether at least one birthday appears more than once.

```{r birthday_function}
birthday_repeated = function(n_people) {
  birthdays = sample(1:365, size = n_people, replace = TRUE)
  repeated = length(unique(birthdays)) < n_people
  return(repeated)
}
```

I run 10,000 simulations for each group size from 2 through 50. Averaging
the logical results estimates the probability of at least one shared birthday.

```{r birthday_simulation}
set.seed(2367)

birthday_results =
  expand_grid(
    n_people = 2:50,
    iteration = 1:10000
  ) |>
  mutate(shared_birthday = map_lgl(n_people, birthday_repeated))

birthday_summary =
  birthday_results |>
  group_by(n_people) |>
  summarize(probability = mean(shared_birthday), .groups = "drop")
```

```{r birthday_plot, fig.cap="Estimated probability of at least one shared birthday, using 10,000 simulations per group size."}
birthday_summary |>
  ggplot(aes(x = n_people, y = probability)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.5, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey60") +
  geom_line(color = "#0072B2") +
  geom_point(color = "#0072B2", size = 1.5) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(2, 10, 20, 30, 40, 50)) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(
    title = "Shared birthdays become more likely in larger groups",
    x = "Number of people",
    y = "Estimated probability"
  )
```

The estimated probability is
`r round(filter(birthday_summary, n_people == 2)$probability, 3)` for two
people, `r round(filter(birthday_summary, n_people == 23)$probability, 3)`
for 23 people, and
`r round(filter(birthday_summary, n_people == 50)$probability, 3)` for 50
people. The probability increases rapidly as the group grows and is around
one half with only 23 people. A match can occur between any pair of people,
not only with one selected person's birthday; the number of possible pairs
increases as the group gets larger. Small simulation fluctuations are
expected because these probabilities are estimated from random samples.

## Problem 2: Longitudinal study

The data come from the [assignment's ZIP archive](https://p8105.com/data/hw5_data.zip).
Each file contains one participant's eight weekly observations. I first
create a dataframe of relative file paths, then use `map` to read each file
into a list column. I extract the arm and subject ID from the filename and
reshape the weekly measurements into long format. Subject IDs are repeated
across arms, so I retain a unique participant identifier combining both.

```{r import_longitudinal_data}
study_data =
  tibble(
    file_path = list.files("data", pattern = "\\.csv$", full.names = TRUE)
  ) |>
  mutate(
    observations = map(file_path, read_csv, show_col_types = FALSE),
    file_name = basename(file_path),
    participant_id = str_remove(file_name, "\\.csv$")
  ) |>
  separate(file_name, into = c("arm", "subject_id"), sep = "_") |>
  mutate(
    subject_id = str_remove(subject_id, "\\.csv$"),
    arm = recode(arm, con = "Control", exp = "Experimental")
  ) |>
  select(-file_path) |>
  unnest(observations) |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = starts_with("week_"),
    names_to = "week",
    names_prefix = "week_",
    values_to = "observation"
  ) |>
  mutate(week = as.integer(week)) |>
  select(participant_id, subject_id, arm, week, observation) |>
  arrange(arm, subject_id, week)
```

The tidy dataset contains `r n_distinct(study_data$participant_id)`
participants and `r nrow(study_data)` participant-week observations, with
`r sum(is.na(study_data$observation))` missing outcome values.

```{r longitudinal_summary}
study_summary =
  study_data |>
  group_by(arm) |>
  summarize(
    participants = n_distinct(participant_id),
    week_1_mean = mean(observation[week == 1]),
    week_8_mean = mean(observation[week == 8]),
    mean_change = week_8_mean - week_1_mean,
    .groups = "drop"
  )

knitr::kable(
  study_summary,
  digits = 2,
  col.names = c("Arm", "Participants", "Week 1 mean", "Week 8 mean", "Mean change"),
  caption = "Group summaries of the longitudinal observations."
)
```

```{r spaghetti_plot, fig.cap="Each line represents one participant; groups are shown on the same vertical scale."}
study_data |>
  ggplot(aes(x = week, y = observation, group = participant_id, color = arm)) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.75, linewidth = 0.6) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.75, size = 1.3) +
  facet_wrap(~arm) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:8) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("Control" = "#0072B2", "Experimental" = "#D55E00")) +
  guides(color = "none") +
  labs(
    title = "Participant trajectories over eight weeks",
    x = "Week",
    y = "Observation"
  )
```

The experimental group generally increases over time, while the control
group fluctuates without a similarly clear upward pattern. The experimental
mean rises from
`r round(filter(study_summary, arm == "Experimental")$week_1_mean, 2)`
to `r round(filter(study_summary, arm == "Experimental")$week_8_mean, 2)`,
a change of
`r round(filter(study_summary, arm == "Experimental")$mean_change, 2)`.
The corresponding control means are
`r round(filter(study_summary, arm == "Control")$week_1_mean, 2)` and
`r round(filter(study_summary, arm == "Control")$week_8_mean, 2)`.
Individual trajectories vary within both groups, but the groups appear
more separated by the end of follow-up. This is a descriptive comparison;
the plot alone does not establish statistical significance or causality.

## Problem 3: Power of a one-sample t-test

For each true mean from 0 through 6, I generate 5,000 independent datasets
with 30 observations from a normal distribution with standard deviation 5.
For each dataset, I conduct a two-sided one-sample t-test of the null
hypothesis that the mean equals zero. I save the estimated mean and p-value
using `broom::tidy`, then define rejection as a p-value below 0.05.

```{r t_test_function}
sim_t_test = function(mu, n = 30, sigma = 5) {
  sample_data = rnorm(n, mean = mu, sd = sigma)

  test_results =
    t.test(sample_data, mu = 0, alternative = "two.sided") |>
    broom::tidy() |>
    select(estimate, p.value)

  return(test_results)
}
```

```{r t_test_simulation}
set.seed(2368)

test_results =
  expand_grid(
    true_mu = 0:6,
    iteration = 1:5000
  ) |>
  mutate(results = map(true_mu, sim_t_test)) |>
  unnest(results) |>
  mutate(rejected = p.value < 0.05)

test_summary =
  test_results |>
  group_by(true_mu) |>
  summarize(
    simulations = n(),
    rejection_rate = mean(rejected),
    mean_estimate = mean(estimate),
    mean_estimate_rejected = mean(estimate[rejected]),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

knitr::kable(
  test_summary,
  digits = 3,
  col.names = c(
    "True mean", "Simulations", "Rejection rate",
    "Mean estimate: all", "Mean estimate: rejected"
  ),
  caption = "Simulation results for two-sided one-sample t-tests."
)
```

```{r power_plot, fig.cap="Rejection rates from 5,000 simulations at each true mean. At a true mean of zero, the rate estimates Type I error rather than power against a false null."}
test_summary |>
  ggplot(aes(x = true_mu, y = rejection_rate)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.05, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey60") +
  geom_line(color = "#0072B2") +
  geom_point(color = "#0072B2", size = 2) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 0:6) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(
    title = "Power increases with the true effect size",
    x = "True mean",
    y = "Proportion of tests rejecting the null"
  )
```

At a true mean of zero, the rejection rate is
`r round(filter(test_summary, true_mu == 0)$rejection_rate, 3)`, close to
the nominal Type I error rate of 0.05. As the true mean moves farther from
zero with sample size and variability held fixed, the standardized effect
size increases and the test has greater power. The estimated power is
`r round(filter(test_summary, true_mu == 2)$rejection_rate, 3)` at a true
mean of 2 and
`r round(filter(test_summary, true_mu == 6)$rejection_rate, 3)` at a true
mean of 6. Larger effects are easier to distinguish from sampling noise.

```{r estimate_plot, fig.cap="Average estimated means across all samples and across samples with significant tests. The dashed line indicates equality with the true mean."}
test_summary |>
  select(true_mu, mean_estimate, mean_estimate_rejected) |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = starts_with("mean_estimate"),
    names_to = "samples",
    values_to = "average_estimate"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    samples = recode(
      samples,
      mean_estimate = "All samples",
      mean_estimate_rejected = "Rejected null only"
    )
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = true_mu, y = average_estimate, color = samples)) +
  geom_abline(intercept = 0, slope = 1, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey50") +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 0:6) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("All samples" = "#0072B2", "Rejected null only" = "#D55E00")) +
  labs(
    title = "Selecting significant tests changes the average estimate",
    x = "True mean",
    y = "Average estimated mean",
    color = NULL
  )
```

Across all samples, the average estimated mean is close to the true mean,
as expected because the sample mean is unbiased. Among samples with
rejected null hypotheses, the average estimate is generally too large for
small positive true means. For example, at a true mean of 1, the average is
`r round(filter(test_summary, true_mu == 1)$mean_estimate, 3)` across all
samples but
`r round(filter(test_summary, true_mu == 1)$mean_estimate_rejected, 3)`
among rejected tests. Conditioning on significance preferentially retains
samples whose estimates are farther from zero relative to their estimated
standard errors. For positive effects with limited power, this selection
mostly favors upward deviations and exaggerates the effect size.

As power approaches one, almost every sample is retained, so the two
averages converge. At a true mean of zero, the two-sided rejection rule is
symmetric: significant positive and negative estimates cancel in
expectation. The signed conditional average is therefore zero in
expectation, although the finite simulation average may differ from zero.
This does not mean individual significant estimates under the null are
small; their absolute magnitudes are selectively large.
